==Problem==
Four congruent semicircles are drawn on the surface of a sphere with radius <imath>2</imath>, as
shown, creating a close curve that divides the surface into two congruent regions.
The length of the curve is <imath>\pi\sqrt{n}</imath>. What is <imath>n</imath>?

[[Image:202310bQ20.jpeg|center]]

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 32 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 12 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 48 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 36 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 27</imath>

==Solution 1==

[[File:AOPSImage1.png | 300px | center]]

Focus on 2 of the points. Let the center of the Sphere be \( A \). Label two points that form the diameter of one of the four semicircles \( M \) and \( C \) respectively. 

Triangle \( AMC \) is a right triangle through the inscribed right triangle theorem, with \( AM = AC = 2 \). 

This is a 45-45-90 triangle, so the length of the diameter \( MC \) is just the hypotenuse of the triangle \( AMC \), which is \( 2\sqrt{2} \). This means the radius is \( \sqrt{2} \). 

The circumference of the semicircle is \( \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2\sqrt{2} \cdot \pi = \pi\sqrt{2} \), and because there are four congruent semicircles, the length of the semicircular region is \( 4\sqrt{2}\pi = \pi \cdot 4\sqrt{2} \). 

The solution is in the form \( \pi\sqrt{n} \), so we convert \( \pi \cdot 4\sqrt{2} \) to \( \pi\sqrt{16}\sqrt{2} \) to get \( \pi\sqrt{32} \). \( n =\)<imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) 32}}</imath>.

~Pinotation

~Diagram by Pinotation

==Solution 2==

There are four marked points on the diagram; let us examine the top two points and call them <imath>A</imath> and <imath>B</imath>. Similarly, let the bottom two dots be <imath>C</imath> and <imath>D</imath>, as shown: 

<asy>
import graph;
import geometry;

unitsize(1cm);

pair A = (-1.41, 1.41);
pair B = (1.41, 1.41);
pair C = (1.41, -1.41);
pair D = (-1.41, -1.41);
pair O = (0, 0);

draw(circle(O,2));
draw(A--O--B,black+dashed);
draw(C--O--D,black+dashed);

dot(A);dot(B);dot(C);dot(D);dot(O);

label("$A$", A, NW);
label("$B$", B, NE);
label("$C$", C, SE);
label("$D$", D, SW);
label("$O$", (0,0.1), N);
</asy>

This is a cross-section of the sphere seen from the side. We know that <imath>{AO}={BO}={CO}={DO}=2</imath>, and by Pythagorean Theorem, length of  <imath>\overline{AB}=2\sqrt2.</imath> 

Each of the four congruent semicircles has the length <imath>AB</imath> as a diameter (since <imath>\overline{AB}</imath> is congruent to <imath>\overline{BC},\overline{CD},</imath> and <imath>\overline{DA}</imath>), so its radius is <imath>\dfrac{2\sqrt2}2=\sqrt2.</imath> Each one's arc length is thus <imath>\pi\cdot\sqrt2=\sqrt2\pi.</imath> 

We have <imath>4</imath> of these, so the total length is <imath>4\sqrt2\pi=\sqrt{32}\pi</imath>, so thus our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }32.}</imath>

~Technodoggo
~minor edits by JiuruAops



Note:

TLDR:

The radius of <imath>2</imath> gives us a line segment connecting diagonal vertices of the semi-circles with a measure of <imath>4</imath>, giving us through <imath>45^{\circ}-45^{\circ}-90^{\circ}</imath> relations and Pythagorean theorem a diameter for each semi-circle of <imath>2\sqrt{2}</imath>, which we can use to bash out the circumference of a full circle, multiply by <imath>2</imath>, and move inside and under the root to get <imath>32</imath>.

~Aryan Mukherjee

== Solution 3 ==
Assume <imath>A</imath>, <imath>B</imath>, <imath>C</imath>, and <imath>D</imath> are the four points connecting the semicircles. By law of symmetry, we can pretty confidently assume that <imath>ABCD</imath> is a square. Then, <imath>\overline{AB} = 2\sqrt2.</imath>, and the rest is the same as the second half of solution <imath>1</imath>.

~jonathanzhou18

==Solution 4==

We put the sphere to a coordinate space by putting the center at the origin.
The four connecting points of the curve have the following coordinates: <imath>A = \left( 0, 0, 2 \right)</imath>, <imath>B = \left( 2, 0, 0 \right)</imath>, <imath>C = \left( 0, 0, -2 \right)</imath>, <imath>D = \left( -2, 0, 0 \right)</imath>.

Now, we compute the radius of each semicircle.
Denote by <imath>M</imath> the midpoint of <imath>A</imath> and <imath>B</imath>. Thus, <imath>M</imath> is the center of the semicircle that ends at <imath>A</imath> and <imath>B</imath>.
We have <imath>M = \left( 1, 0, 1 \right)</imath>.
Thus, <imath>OM = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}</imath>.

In the right triangle <imath>\triangle OAM</imath>, we have <imath>MA = \sqrt{OA^2 - OM^2} = \sqrt{2}</imath>.

Therefore, the length of the curve is
<cmath>
\begin{align*}
4 \cdot \frac{1}{2} 2 \pi \cdot MA
= \pi \sqrt{32} .
\end{align*}
</cmath>

Therefore, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) 32}}</imath>.

~Steven Chen (Professor Chen Education Palace, www.professorchenedu.com)

==Solution 5==
Note that each of the diameters are the chord of the sphere of a quarter arc. Thus, the semicircles diameter's length is <imath>2\sqrt{2}</imath>. Thus, the entire curve is <imath>2\sqrt{2} \cdot \pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 = 4\sqrt{2} \pi = \sqrt{32} \pi</imath>. Therefore, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) 32}}</imath>.
~andliu766

==Solution 6 (Cheese! Narrow it down to 2 choices!) and actual way (this one is stupid)==
Cheese: You can immediately say that the answer choice is either <imath>{\text{(A) }32}</imath> or <imath>{\text{(C) }48}</imath> because there are four semicircles in that curve; there are <imath>4 = \sqrt{16}</imath> semicircles in the curve, so n has to be a multiple of 16, and if you don't know how to do this problem, just guess one of <imath>{\text{(A)}}</imath> or <imath>{\text{(C)}}</imath>.
Actual way: Take a cross-section of the sphere to get four different points equidistant from the center <imath>O</imath> of the sphere, <imath>A</imath>, <imath>B</imath>, <imath>C</imath>, <imath>D</imath> such that <imath>AO = BO = CO = DO = 2</imath>, and so <imath>ABCD</imath> is a square with side length <imath>2\sqrt{2}</imath>, and proceed as in Solution 2 to get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) 32}}</imath>.
